 The case for less optimization in baseball
 Give us a degree of uncertainty, it’s worth it.
 by Joshua Diemert Oct 27, 2026, 5:00 PM UTC Facebook 
 Link 
 If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. 
 MILWAUKEE, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 24: Yandy Diaz #2 of the Tampa Bay Rays strikes out for the final out against the Milwaukee Brewers to end the ninth inning in game two of the 2026 World Series at American Family Field on October 24, 2026 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) Getty Images Joshua Diemert has been writing at Pinstripe Alley since April 2017, in a perpetual search for a more perfect understanding of what value is. Game 2 of the 2026 World Series ended, to some, in controversy. Yandy Díaz may, or may not, have checked his swing in a full count facing Aaron Ashby , getting himself punched out as the Brewers went up 2-0 in the Fall Classic. The called strike three set off a round of assurances that the check swing challenge system being tested in the minor leagues will fix this, that we will have a perfect game soon.
 I’m not sure I want a perfect game. I’m not sure I want a perfect anything .
 I wrote almost two years ago as the ABS system loomed on the horizon about preserving a tinge of doubt. That challenge system has turned out great. The most egregious calls, especially earlier in the season, were corrected, but limits on how many reviews you get and internal controls on who and when you can challenge introduced a new layer of in-game tactical decisions, adding friction to the newly-optimized strikezone.
 That balance is the one that I’m increasingly interested in finding. Everything is very easy for us now. I can write this from my toilet while on a lunch break from my email job with a burrito in a heat bag on the back of a bicycle about to be dropped off outside my door. The perpetual optimization of the consumer life has made it easier to do nothing but stay home and consume, but has removed bumping into a friend walking down the street or seeing a cool bird because you had to walk through the park to get food yourself.
 The increase in LLM usage underscores this as well. Once again I give a pledge to you all that you will never read a word of mine that came from Claude or Chat or any of the New C Words, but I work with people and text (a limited amount) with people and read essays from people that involve a prompt, and maybe a follow-up, and no sweat or creativity afterward. These things cause me great pain to read.
 Baseball’s path to optimization hasn’t really made people more stagnant in the same way that DoorDash and streaming services have. Instead, the path to optimization has resulted in the thing that I believe is hurting the watchability of the sport: pitching is too good. We have learned how to add three miles per hour to everyone’s pitch, with an extra three inches of horizontal break to every sweeper, three inches of induced vertical break to everyone’s fastball, we’ve figured out tunneling so the three pitches a reliever features all look the same until past the swing decision point, and we’ve worked out that using five pitchers in a nine-inning game is more effective on a per-inning basis than three.
 Indeed, one major reason why the Brewers and Rays are in the World Series in the first place is because they have so managed to optimize pitching. Between Jacob Misiorowski and Freddy Peralta and Aaron Ashby and Drew Rassmussen, this is what you get when you’ve hit the absolute prime in development. The only way to claw any of that back is institutional — I’m in favor of both limiting the number of pitchers you have on your roster, and tying the DH to pitcher usage in some way, but this post isn’t about that.
 It’s about baseball losing friction. Once everything is optimized yes we should have a game where everything is decided solely by the players and … OK, yeah, sure, but that also means we never get a Jeffrey Maier, or a Jackie-and-Yogi at home plate, indelible moments of baseball’s history. Sports are meant to have a little mess, just a little, because that’s what we end up talking about.
 Last Friday I saw the newly-restored remaster of Ken Russell’s The Devils , one of the more controversial and explicit pieces of film ever made. It was a little inconvenient to get there, as the bus we had to take is the least reliable bus line in the city, the mall the cinema is attached to is very much a liminal space with an elevator that has over the summer induced vertigo more than once. I could have stayed home, pulled up a torrent, watched it on TV not five feet from the desk where I work a full-time job.
 But I didn’t, and the experience was better for it. Rolling my eyes at an unreliable bus leads to widening them at Sister Jean cloaked entirely in shadow. Forgoing the free torrent for a paid showing meant whoa I’ve never heard the score like that .
 We want optimization, and we should get a good amount of it. This Series is the showcase of the uber-optimized ballclub though, and forgive me for preferring to argue whether Jackie was really out at home plate — and he was.
